findings.evidence: The dbff837f digest is a cut list (showing 40 of 61). Record rows cover the section ids those units belong to, including accepted drops for s006 and s009 and a stale drop for s008, but the 21 unshown paragraphs have no item of their own.
findings.fix: List the 21 unshown para ids in docs/audit/recovery/compose-email/record.md, each with an allowed fate, value and decision, or restore any still-missing template or rule into the bundled professional-communication skill.

findings.evidence: Body: bullets only for 3-5 parallel points (never more), bold the one key fact, keep paragraphs to 2-3 sentences.
findings.fix: Keep the non-obvious rules (subject tags, proposed-date labelling, disclosure, placeholders). Move the generic bullet, bold and paragraph limits to skills/professional-communication/references/ and load that file only when formatting a long body.

findings.evidence: Purpose tie-breaks pack Request, Follow-up, Escalation, Status, FYI, thank-you, announcement and introduction into one paragraph, then restate the same leads as a second list.
findings.fix: Make step 2(c) one ordered decision list, each purpose once, with its lead and its closing, so the procedure is the pattern instead of a paragraph plus a menu.

findings.evidence: In extension or scope requests, offer the trade-off (new date, or cut scope to keep the date) so the reader can decide.
findings.fix: State the failure mode: a request that offers only a new date lets the reader treat scope as unchanged, so name both options and who chooses.

findings.evidence: Description: Not for casual chat replies; a finished draft can be reformatted for Slack or Teams on request.
findings.fix: Draft or rewrite a professional email to a peer, stakeholder, manager or leadership using What-Why-How. Use for status updates, approval requests, escalations, follow-ups, deadline extensions, or when the user only asks to make a message shorter, clearer or less defensive, even without the word email. Produces a subject and body to paste; never sends. Not for Slack or Teams chat replies, meeting notes or documents; a finished email draft can be reformatted for Slack or Teams only when the user asks.

findings.evidence: Step 2(c) says otherwise Status when the message is a progress report, and FYI for other informational messages, while the purpose bullets repeat Status and FYI leads and step 5 then changes which caps apply.
findings.fix: Give one default per purpose: Request, Escalation and Follow-up use the What 1-2 and Why 2-3 caps; Status and FYI use the user's voice inside the 150-word default. State each once.

findings.evidence: Ten scenarios cover the main path and failures (empty invocation, send refusal, word-limit overflow), but none asserts the disputed-claim reply, the disclosure redaction, or the leadership 5-sentence cap.
findings.fix: Add one scenario whose assertions check that a sender's disputed date stays attributed, internal logs are withheld and named, and a leadership draft stays within five sentences.

findings.evidence: Step 1 says a missing recipient name, date or outcome is not blocking and to infer audience and outcome, while the same step says if nothing at all is known, ask for the recipient and the desired outcome, then stop.
findings.fix: Define the stop condition as no topic and no source draft and no received message. When a topic is known, infer audience and outcome and draft, using a placeholder only for a missing recipient name or date.

findings.evidence: If the source facts cannot fit a stated word limit, keep every fact, report the overage and ask (blocking); the only worked example is an extension request whose facts fit, so the overflow branch has no outcome.
findings.fix: Add a short overflow example that reports the word count, names the facts at risk, asks whether to relax the limit or drop named items, and shows no draft until the user answers.
